Of course, you can always just leave the colours at their default value, which would be my recommendation, but in my opinion it's better to have too many choices as opposed to too few. notes.title: Weekly Update #127: Base Classes and Advanced Classes
notes.notes:
Hey all! Today I want to briefly talk about class progression, and how certain classes are accessed over the course of the game. While we do allow you to change a unit's class very freely, the list of classes that a unit has access to will start smaller and expand over time as you gain more ranks in different classes.

Essentially, we have a distinction between 'base' classes, which any unit can switch to at any time, and 'advanced' classes, which require experience in certain classes, or other special requirements to be met. Don't be misled by the names we've given them; advanced classes aren't necessarily stronger than base classes. Every one of our classes are designed to be competitive throughout the duration of the game. Advanced classes, however, often have more complex or specialized kits, which can make them stronger in certain situations.

Most of the planned base classes have been revealed already, such as Knight, Lumimancer, Archer, Thief and Pyromancer. Advanced classes that we've revealed include Berserker, Enchanter and Templar. These classes will be inaccessible to a unit unless they have reached a certain class rank on specific classes. For example, accessing Templar requires reaching rank 5 in Lumimancer and rank 3 in Knight.

Advanced classes will not appear on the reclass menu initially, but once one of the unlock conditions has been met we'll provide a hint, such as a silhouette, which should encourage players to experiment and discover advanced classes naturally. We've tried to ensure that prerequisite classes make sense where possible, like with Templar incorporating aspects of both the Knight and Lumimancer classes (high survivability, heavy armor/weapons and light magic). Of course, this is all still in development, so most of it is subject to change, especially the unlock requirements for classes.

notes.title: Weekly Update #124: Skill Selection and Target Preview
notes.notes:
Hey all! Here's a first look at a new menu I've been working on. I've been doing a ton of research recently and have a bunch of new ideas for how to improve some aspects of Crystal Horizons, primarily focusing on the UI. Recently, I've been trying to improve the Action Menus, which are a little bit important seeing as they are your primary point of interaction in the game.

Since the very beginning of the project, we've been using a design that involves small vertical menus that kind of fold out from the bottom right of the screen, pushing older submenus further left as you navigate through them. While there are some upsides to a layout like this, I constantly felt restricted when trying to convey information to the player. There's only so much space for information, and I cannot stress how important it is that a player has access to as much valuable information as possible as efficiently as possible.

So, after a few failed attempts at making the old design work, I've moved on to a new layout. At this stage, we'll still be using the vertical menu for the first level of the action menu, which has options like Move, Attack, Skills and Items. I'm looking into something new for that too, but it isn't ready just yet. For options like Skills, previously we would open another vertical menu for skill categories (for example, Archer would have Archery, Elemental Quiver and Bow Arts as options), which would then open a third menu with all of the actual skills.

[img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44901040/ad746b390269f7c627389a16bf6845a8825e06e8.png"]

With this new design, however, I've managed to streamline the process into a single larger menu. Upon selecting Skills, you'll now open the Skill Menu, which has lists of skills just like before. Instead of being under different menus, requiring navigating back and forth through different levels, we now have other skill categories as separate tabs that can be accessed with a simple left or right input. Most importantly however, we're able to include a lot more information. I'm very excited about this, but nothing here excites me as much as the Target Preview.

This little thing has been on my wishlist for years now, but I could never find a place for it that was both useful and easily accessible. Playtests have shown that attack range and area of effect are often some of the most confusing things for players to understand on a skill-by-skill basis. Now, when selecting a skill to use, you'll be able to get a strong idea of how the skill works without needing to select the skill and begin the targeting phase. This should make some of our more unique skills a bit less confusing to use.

As always, we'll be looking to make small improvements here and there and clean up any errors. In fact, we've already made the panel a little bit smaller since we got the screenshots, but you'll have to wait until next week to see the difference. Additionally, we'll need to create some simple icons for the different skill categories, as right now I'm just reusing old status icons and the weapon icons. I'll be sitting on this one for a while and seeing what feedback I get and how it goes in tests, but I'm a big fan of the design personally so I have high hopes. Thanks as always for tuning in!

notes.title: Weekly Update #118: Progress Report - Part 2
notes.notes:
Hey all! We're working through a lot of the things we talked about in last week's progress update, and while we are making progress I don't have anything from that ready in time for this week's update. I was hoping to have the updated status icons ready, but I'm not quite satisfied with their current iteration. While I keep working on getting those prepared, I thought it might be a good idea to do a kind of 'part 2' for the progress report, this time focusing on some areas of development that don't get talked about much here.

While most of our updates revolve around the battle scene, as that's where most of our development time is spent right now, we do have some temporary layouts for other out-of-battle menus. These have been drafted using whatever assets we have around right now, and are primarily for our own personal reference until we get to working directly on them. As such, they're not really fit to be shown off yet, but once we make more progress on diversifying our collection of UI assets I'll be able to update them and share.

Apart from that, I wanted to give a relatively brief update on the story of Crystal Horizons. We've talked briefly about it here and there in early updates, but haven't really said much in a while. So, allow me to share with you where we're at with the game's script.

Currently, we have the overall scenario written and mostly finalized; there's still some room for small adjustments if needed but it's pretty well locked in right now. We're currently going through and fleshing out details for major characters in the story, and making any needed adjustments to the scenario based on that. As for character dialogue, while we have drafted a not insignificant number of scenes (especially for the earlier sections of the game), nothing is really finalized at this stage, as we're primarily working through the previous two stages first.

As I said before, most of our development time is spent on the battle scene right now. This is of course due to our current highest priority being preparing and holding our beta test, but that doesn't mean we've been entirely neglecting out-of-battle tasks. One task we'll be tackling in the near future will be creating a proper, high quality world map for the game, which we intend to use on at least one of those out-of-battle menus. Once we have that asset, as well as a few more character portraits, we'll be able to go back to talking about the world and story a bit more frequently.

That's all I can share this week; I'm planning to have those status icons ready for next week, and I'm hoping the before-and-after comparison will blow you all away! Until then, thanks for tuning in!

notes.title: Weekly Update #117: Progress Report - Mid 2025
notes.notes:
Hey all! It's been a little while since our last big progress report, so I think now is a good time to share where we're at and what our priorities are for the next stage of development.

To start with, here's a quick recap of what we've been up to since our last progress update:

All main UI pieces (menus, windows, etc.) for the battle scene have had their layout updated and all but the Glossary are completely functional

Our eight beta classes have all their basic (non unique/skill) attack animations either completed or drafted and displaying in game

Additional revealed classes have class icons and base sprites either completed or drafted, but not attack animations

We've made some more battle maps, one of which we're showing off soon in another update after revealing it three weeks ago

There's probably more, but those are the main things we've done recently. There's a few things that I've left out, and that's because I want to go into a bit more detail now.

First off, status icons. We've shown off our status icons in a lot of weekly updates in the past. They are something that is usually pretty easy to get footage/screenshots of and talk about when compared to things like game systems, which is where a lot of our time goes. That said, some of the icons, especially the recently shown off Berserker icons for Shredded and Savagery, aren't quite up to standard.

[img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44901040/9770873233f275c499c78ce49a74cf51ae7f1f0e.png"]

Our overall lukewarm opinion of those icons led us to discuss and review all our icons and the artstyle we're using for them. As a result, we identified a number of weaknesses and possible improvements that could be made, and marked a not insignificant number of both old and new status icons for improvements. Our goal is to maintain the current artstyle while loosening up a bit on certain restrictions and improving overall quality. Once we're happy with the results, we'll share some before and after comparisons.

This task should be relatively easy and not eat up too much development time in other areas, as it's something that can be done on its own at any time. I'll be working on it inbetween other major tasks.

One of those major tasks is expanding our VFX systems. So far, all our visual effects have been made by hand using Unity's VFX Graph, but we've had to accept that we don't really have the skill and manpower to keep that up right now. As such, we're currently in the process of transitioning to pre-made visual effects, which we've acquired in great quantity and quality. The plan for now is to use these new effects where appropriate, and modify or create custom VFX for more specific skills.

Whether we stick with the pre-made effects or eventually replace them all with custom effects isn't something we can decide right now. Once we have them working as intended in the battle scene, I'll share new gameplay videos with the new effects (and likely some other additional things we've done that haven't been seen since our last video). This is a task we've already started working on and are prioritizing right now.

[img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44901040/c92e9fa3ea6c26f9b345176c054789d5859c9b4c.gif"]

Finally, we have to address the lack of both UI and character art assets. As mentioned in the last update about the Glossary, we're currently too reliant on the few UI assets we have, and are looking into additional assets. I'd put this at medium priority right now; we definitely need to expand our options before progressing too much further. This task will require a lot of iteration though, so it might be a while before we have anything definitive to share.

As for character art, I can't really say much more than 'we're working on it'. Our team lacks any professionally trained artists, and while we have been able to produce some character art in the past, we're painfully aware that the quality is lacking. On top of everything we're already doing, we're also training some members of our team in character art and are trying to reach a certain level of quality as quickly as possible. I'd love to say that we'll have something ready soon, but for now we'll have to wait and see.

That's all I've got to share today. I want to genuinely thank everyone who's still with us throughout development. We're a small team working on this game as best we can in our spare time, and while I know development is painfully slow at times, I'm extremely grateful for your support. We'll keep doing our best to bring updates to you all, so thanks for tuning in!

notes.title: Weekly Update #116: Glossary V2 - First Look
notes.notes:
Hey all! We've made some pretty notable progress on updating the Glossary, the massive repository of information that can be accessed at any time. The screenshots I'll be sharing this week have been taken while the Glossary is in a state of 'not quite working right now', so while the layout is done it doesn't quite connect to the battle scene just yet. That will be the next step after making any further adjustments to overall layout, and then we'll get to add nice animations for opening, closing and navigating the Glossary.

[img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44901040/57c77f4bc9a240706c1384991930f94fc30df2f8.png"]

The first major change from the old Glossary is the introduction of a new landing screen. Previously, the glossary would open straight into a contents view which you would be able to scroll up and down through, but now we start on a simpler page with eight options to choose from. Most glossary entries will be sorted into the first five categories: Guide, Classes, Tiles, Items and World. The Skill Index and Status Index will provide A-Z lists of all skills or statuses in the game for quick navigation and reference, while the Recent category will provide a list of all entries that were recently made available.

[img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44901040/06bcd42ec61df95bea08f244cd3bef3fabfa0b7f.png"]

Upon selecting a category, we navigate to a view more reminiscent of the previous Glossary. We've adjusted the proportions and layout of the Glossary to be less overwhelming, and provided quick navigation buttons to other categories. Additionally, different entries might have slightly different layouts, such as statuses displaying their icons.

[img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44901040/dee02945a13507a057bc1e0e560752ef497059e7.png"]

Now, for the elephant in the room, I am aware that we have maybe three total unique assets in use here. If you didn't think we were overusing the blue gradient box asset before, then this should make it more clear than ever. We'll be spending some time in the near future diversifying our UI assets, so you can expect the design to change a bit once we've done that. Layout-wise, I'm pretty happy with how it looks, but it's definitely in need of some visual variety.

That's all I've got for this week, though. Next time I show off the Glossary, it should be fully integrated into the game and have a greater variety of assets, so look forward to that! When it happens.

Also, one quick announcement: Team Whirlwind unfortunately won't be exhibiting at AVCon this year. We're very behind on some of our goals (which I probably don't need to say) and decided that our time would be better spent working towards those instead of creating a new demo and doing all the fun preparation required for that and AVCon. Hopefully the beta will make up for that, so we're working full speed on everything needed to get there. Thanks as always for your support, and I'll keep you updated on that front!

Hey all! Allow me to introduce a new addition to the Tile Panel in the top left; we now have custom icons for unique Tile Effects! Here we have Guard Aura, the passive defense buff granted by Knights, and Sanctified, a lingering healing effect placed by the Lumimancer's Sanctuary spell. {STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44901040/0bb5f4001ba4aeda02a6a85e74a67c9d6e1849c5.png

There isn't really a limit to how many unique tile effects can be affecting a single tile at once, so I thought some icons would help break up the text and make it easier to recognize what's going on when lots of effects are in play. Originally, we did consider having visual effects on the tiles themselves, but that would add far too much visual clutter. notes.title: Weekly Update #101: Master Skills, Part 2
notes.notes:
Hey all! This week is a follow-up to last week's introduction of Master Skills, going over some details I feel I missed or didn't explain enough. I'll also provide some insight into the concepting and creation of Master Skills.

The first thing I'll touch on is the Mastery gauge, the HUD element used to represent a unit's current Mastery resource. While it was visible in last week's clips, I didn't bring any attention to it, so I wanted to explain what the additional bar on the Unit Info Panel was and clear up an error I left in the clip (in the Seraphim clip where it appeared empty for a bit).

Once we figure out exactly how we want to lay it out, we'll likely add a numerical value like the other resource bars and breaks every 20%, to maintain parity with the Focus (FP) bar due to their interconnectivity. While we like the current design for the gauge, we might make further adjustments, as it was the final thing added before capturing the gameplay footage.

Now, where did the ideas for Master Skills come from, and why were they only revealed recently? Originally, many of our classes capped off their rank progression with a cool, powerful skill at Rank 10. Things like Knight's Heavensfall and Lumimancer's Radiant Ray; awesome skills to reward the player for sticking with a class all the way to the end, with great power and great resource costs as well. While these 'capstone' skills were cool in theory, in practice they interrupted the flow of gaining and spending FP too much, and weren't really satisfying to use.

That's not even mentioning the cost of remaining on a class already at max rank. We've made reclassing as simple and painless as possible to encourage players to build out a diverse array of options, and choosing to stay on a rank 10 class means not gaining rank EXP on another class, which might slow down acquisition of advanced classes (as a refresher, some classes require the unit have other classes at a certain rank or above in order to access).

So, we had all these amazing ideas for big, flashy skills, but they didn't fit into the gameplay loop cleanly on both a macro and micro level. That meant going back to the drawing board, figuring out if we could salvage these skills or if we would have to change them drastically. It was by looking at the core issue with FP that we began to iterate on our current solution; incorporate the skills into the core gameplay loop of building and spending FP.

Taking skills we previously intended to be powerful, end-of-progression things and making them available at rank 1 did require some changes to be made. In order to maintain the idea of providing a cool reward to the player for hitting max rank, the solution we came to was to have the skill increase in power at rank 10, meaning some skills were stripped back a bit at rank 1 before being upgraded back into their original concept at max rank. We also added an upgrade point at rank 5, both because rank 5 is a pretty important rank (for reasons which I'll discuss in a future update, maybe?) and so we could scale the skill up a bit more smoothly over all 10 ranks.

That's all I've got for now, though! I'm always happy to talk through some of our design intentions and processes (maybe a bit too happy, this was meant to be a short update). Closed beta test is still on the way, although I still can't give a definitive date. Development has been a lot more challenging than any of us expected, but we're as committed as ever, and I'll share any news I can when I can! Thanks for tuning in!

notes.title: Weekly Update #100: Master Skills
notes.notes:
Hey all! Here it is, the big 100th update! We've been posting development updates for almost two whole years now, and I sometimes find myself looking back to see how far the project has come. Recent updates have been a bit slow, mostly various UI changes and the like. But now, it is my pleasure to introduce you all to a core game mechanic that we've been working on for a long time now: Master Skills!

Alongside Skills, Spells and Weaponskills, Master Skills are another type of activated ability, requiring their own resource to be built up before use. This resource, which we're calling Mastery at the moment, is built up by spending Focus (FP) at a one-to-one ratio. Using a Master Skill requires reaching 100% Mastery, and consumes the entire resource upon use. These skills are extremely powerful, limited by how few times per battle you'll get to use them; anywhere from 0-2 times depending on the length of the battle.

Due to the resource being gained by spending FP, this means that classes which generate and spend FP quicker will get to use their Master Skills more often. Similarly, classes that generate FP slower (such as spellcasters like Lumimancer and Pyromancer) will get to use theirs less. We've taken this into account and designed each class' Master Skill with the frequency of use in mind, leading slower classes to have generally stronger skills.

Each class gets access to only one Master Skill, available from Rank 1. At certain class ranks, the Master Skill receives slight enhancements, such as increasing range or adding an additional buff/debuff on hit. While most of the skills are still in development and unable to be shown off, I do have two I can talk about today: Lumimancer and Pyromancer! As spellcasters, they have skills which are both strong and awesome, so I figured there was no better way to introduce the mechanic than with some of the coolest!

[previewyoutube=jBiGeK2H4gM;full][/previewyoutube]

First, we have Lumimancer and the Seraphim skill! This skill creates a seraphic avatar out of light, which fires three devastating beams onto targeted areas! Much like Flash, the standard Lumimancer spell, this skill also deals damage to enemies while healing allies. While it does hit three times, it can only affect the same unit once per use, so dropping all three beams on one enemy will be pretty ineffective (it was really funny before we changed it though).

At later ranks, Seraphim gets upgraded to apply Illuminated to enemies. Since this skill can target up to 15 tiles under optimal conditions, it has the potential to be extremely strong, so we'll be keeping an eye on the power level. It also has a much longer range than other Lumimancer options, so its bound to find use when you need it most!

Pyromancer gets access to the destructive power of Worldrazer, a massive area-of-effect damage Master Skill. Worldrazer summons down a flaming meteor, dealing extreme damage in a huge area. Much like Pyromancer's other spells, the meteor does not care for whom it annihilates; ally or enemy alike. In the aftermath, expect the ground to be burned and barren having been Scorched, a tile effect that reduces incoming healing and deals damage upon movement through the tile.

Those who survive the impact will find themselves similarly burned, taking additional damage at the start of their turns. Worldrazer is truly a force of complete destruction, and is thankfully limited by the slow rate of FP generation that Pyromancer suffers from. At higher ranks, Worldrazer gains additional power based on how many stacks of Rings of Infernum the caster has, among other effects.

Alongside the skills being functional in-game, we've also made some improvements to our VFX systems and workflow; we're now able to animate a few more things, including the camera! Right now, we're using it primarily for Master Skills, to truly sell the scale and scope of the skill. I've included some early looks at the visual effects for both Seraphim and Worldrazer today, and while we wouldn't exactly say they're finished, I hope they can give you an idea of just how powerful these skills are meant to be.

Once we have a few more completed, I'll put together a video showcasing the Master Skills for our eight Beta classes, but until then I ask for your patience. Please look forward to more looks at these powerful skills in the future, and thanks for tuning in! 

(Showcase clips muted, haven't done sound effects yet. Apologies, please enjoy the VFX regardless!)

notes.title: Weekly Update #99: Maps Left Behind
notes.notes:
Hey all! This week, I'm diving deep into the project files to look through some old maps we created! These were created using our Terrain to Map tool, which converts the heightmap of a Unity terrain to a map for Crystal Horizons, even including things like slopes! We've shown off this tool in action before, but today we're looking at some of the maps we made that didn't quite make the cut. These were made shortly after the creation of the conversion tool, while we were still seeing what it could do and testing its limits, so come with me on a little adventure across three different forgotten maps!

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44901040/3e9db0b0e4e31df51e81716627982655f5b5dfbc.png

First up, we have this desert-like map. When maps are first generated, we give them two tile materials to use; one for tiles exposed to the air, like grass, and one to make up walls and other covered tiles, like dirt. Adding variance to the tiles comes a few steps later, so these maps didn't get that far, meaning they only have one or two tile textures on each. For this map, it means a lot of sand.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44901040/a594ec8b16ae2bcbc782a7eac2525f712abf741e.png

For the most part, the overall map is fine. The hill in the center and the valley that goes around it may be a bit too steep for interesting combat to take place, but with some adjustments it could definitely come back later down the line. Our second map today, however, is a bit more unique.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44901040/81b603998eb3d2055d038b23375b69566e965932.png

This flowery map has some interesting spires that dominate most of the map, with a plateau in the corner. With lots of high ground and cover, this could lead to some interesting interactions with ranged classes like Stormcaller and Archer, but there are some problems with it. Most notably, with single-tile raised areas like with the spires, it's possible for a unit to jump up and then be unable to be attacked by melee units due to the attack height limit.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44901040/c48410767f42faddf8b89c298b60990e588dc8ec.png

I suspect that this map was made primarily to test how sharp spikes in the terrain would behave with the conversion tool. Observing how the tiles ended up being placed, and how slopes were distributed, could have led to us having a better idea of how to create terrain to more accurately convert to the maps we wanted. I can see potential for this map, but it would likely need some major adjustments and a lot of playtesting to get to a good state.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44901040/e1a198abf3656afb54eebf60accb05a3ce6dab10.png

Now, our final map today is a big one. Easily the biggest one we've ever made, and a clear limit test for our conversion tool (and my poor PC). This mountain map is massive, and features a relatively linear path from down below, underneath a bridge, up a slope and then to the top layer of the map. Big maps with multiple layers are definitely things we wanted to try, but as we've learnt more about map size, enemy density and how combat actually plays out, it's become more and more difficult to justify designing a map like this.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44901040/efd4258c168dfaa162f92ec1c3407d7cebedc128.png

That's not to mention all the issues with visibility; we've got some tricks to make objects on the map less intrusive, but moving your units through a small space surrounded by walls would get very confusing, very fast. While this map is cool, especially owing to its scale, it's simply not a design that would lead to a fun, satisfying playable experience. Still, its sitting around in the project files, so maybe we'll find some way to use it in the future.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44901040/b5625a3c6e61ea7949316e18d13c595c4e611930.png

That'll be all for this week! Look forward to the next update; it's going to be a big one!

notes.title: Weekly Update #95: Class Design Insights, Part 2
notes.notes:
This week will be a short continuation of last week's update, as I quickly go over some other class changes we're making. We focused on the Lumimancer class last time, but today I'm looking at Thief. It might not be surprising to see that the most notable adjustments are for our oldest classes, with newer designs like Enchanter and Berserker seeing minimal tweaks.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44901040/37b48d4dfc01ec67ca74f951220ea69e5b0c067c.png

So, to go back a bit, after AVCon we determined that Thief was in need of some gameplay updates. When the class was first designed, we wanted to focus on having a class that built up to dealing massive burst damage, stacking boosts over multiple turns and striking from weak points. To this end, the class was designed to function without a Move skill, having both Fade Out and Sharpen be standard skills.

In a vacuum, this didn't feel too bad, but when compared to other classes like Knight, Archer and Enchanter, not having a Move skill that tied into the class' rotation made it feel a lot slower, considering it's big damage attack only happened once every three turns. While we did discuss having a Move skill before AVCon, we were concerned about how strong it could be on a class with extremely high speed and decided to leave it until after testing.

Some of our discussions immediately following public playtests led us to the idea of adding in a Move skill that required certain conditions to use, but would allow Thief to reapply one of it's buffs. In a weekly update back in July, we mentioned how we were looking as allowing them to reapply Elusive, the critical damage multiplier and evasion buff, after landing a critical hit with a Dirty Fighting skill. After more iteration, here's what we're looking at now:

Two new skills have been added to the Thief's kit; the Move skill Tumble and the passive skill Unseen Strike. Tumble costs 20 FP, but allows the Thief to roll up to two tiles in any direction, even through enemies, but with a vertical movement of 0.5 tiles. Essentially, this means they can roll up and down slopes but can't jump within the movement. Using Tumble will apply Elusive for two turns, as opposed to the four granted by using Fade Out, but will allow the class to maintain a strong flow in battle.

Unseen Strike is a passive skill that grants the Unseen status to the Thief upon successfully hitting a Dirty Fighting skill from the correct positional. This status allows the Thief to use Tumble for 0 FP, essentially making it a free Move action. With this combination of skills, the class should be able to set up with Fade Out before getting within range of an enemy, then build FP with enhanced basic attacks, spend FP on Dirty Fighting skills, and roll to reapply Elusive for the enhanced critical damage and evasion. Tumble will be available on the class' base kit, while Unseen Strike will be unlocked at Rank 4.

There's been some other small changes to the kit in response to these additions, which we'll be watching carefully, and hopefully be able to show off in-game sooner rather than later. These last two updates have been walls of text, but next week I'll be sure to get some screenshots of some of the other things we've been working on in-engine. It's not ideal, but when we need an update every week, some of them have to be a bit less full than others. Still, I hope you're looking forward to trying out the updated classes, especially if you've played before! Thanks for tuning in!

notes.title: Weekly Update #94: Class Design Insights
notes.notes:
Hey all! One of the things we're most confident in with Crystal Horizons, enough to name it as a core pillar of the game, is our class design. The complex, interconnected kits are unique among other games in the genre, taking inspiration from modern MMORPG design to elevate the identity of a class and add another layer of strategic decision making. I bring this up because I want to share the results of our playtesting and discussion regarding class kits, and highlight a few changes that we're testing with some classes.

We'll be focusing on Lumimancer today, but I might continue this with some of the other classes we've adjusted next week. Let's take a look at how the class started, our design philosophy for classes, and how we've evolved the class to where it is today.

Lumimancer is, at it's core, the primary healing class in Crystal Horizons. Other healing classes (not yet revealed but maybe soon?) may have certain restrictions on their healing such as range, area, or resource requirements. Unlike those classes, Lumimancer has a simple yet effective kit; Flash allows for ranged single-target healing or damage, Sacrament allows for ranged multi-target healing, and Rejuvenation grants a regeneration buff to allies in an area. Chuck in a few damage and utility spells as well and you have a solid, useful skillset that would be perfectly fine in a tactics game.

(Here's a side-by-side of the Lumimancer spell list, from one of our earliest builds next to current. Surprisingly, most spells have survived to the current iteration, although their effects have changed a lot.)

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44901040/ebe18f05818873c2ff4a59f95552ff8d33837790.png
{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44901040/ce713ff3e80684ae3d5d3c05dfbed6e760312efe.png

Here in Crystal Horizons, though? That kind of simplicity simply doesn't fit alongside other classes on the field. Our intention is for players to be able to use their mastery of a class to set up and execute on complex strategies over multiple turns. To this end, we try to look at how well a class can act both reactively and proactively. Right now, our simple Lumimancer doesn't have much in the way of proactive gameplay, apart from applying regen and doing damage. So, how do we go about adjusting this base to be more in-line with our design goals?

The easiest way to do so is to introduce a status of some kind that allows different parts of the class to interact with each other. In this case, we have Illuminated. Illuminated is a debuff with a relatively simple purpose; be applied by some skills and consumed to power up others. Our first iteration of this had it be applied through area-of-effect spells (Luminous Impulse, Word of Law) and consumed by single-target spells (Flash, Judgement) to increase their damage.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44901040/6ea0b739f9161d13c36919e7e6c906d324e32ce4.gif

While the damage-dealing aspect of the class was now better, we also wanted to address healing. Healing often felt dissatisfying to do when compared to dealing damage, so we created the Blessing passive to bridge that gap. Now, any healing spells would additionally apply Blessed to healed allies, which granted them additional healing based on damage done by the Lumimancer that applied it. Now a Lumimancer can apply buffs and deal damage, apply regen and Blessed before damage is even taken, and keep allies healthy while still dealing damage.

This iteration of the class is what we brought to AVCon 2024, but there were still some pain points. Luminous Impulse was far too strong, being the correct choice for damage 90% of the time. Some skills such as Holy Ward were barely used, given the value that regeneration brought in comparison to a defense buff, and Flash was basically never used as people opted to use Luminous Impulse for damage and Sacrament for healing.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44901040/e79f00b9607175926df097527cb74ec4651c6275.gif

We want to shift the power around a bit without damaging the fantasy of the class; Luminous Impulse feels really good to use, and seeing massive damage numbers when Judgement hits an Illuminated target feels amazing. So, the changes we're currently testing involve weakening Luminous Impulse at base by lowering its damage and removing its ability to apply Illuminated. Instead, Flash will now apply Illuminated, alongside the more restrictive line AoE spell Word of Law, while Luminous Impulse, Judgement and Shining Jail will consume Illuminated to deal more damage (and extend the duration of Jailed for Shining Jail).

Illuminated now also increases accuracy against the affected unit, and allows the aforementioned spells to bypass accuracy checks when targeting Illuminated targets (guaranteeing they hit). This allows us to be a bit harsher on the base accuracy of Luminous Impulse and Judgement if we need to, giving us more ways to balance the spells once we get down to fine-tuning them. We also buffed Holy Ward, granting additional Block Rate (% chance to halve incoming damage) as well as defense.

We'll be testing these changes in the coming weeks, and you'll likely see some iteration of them when we hold the beta (soon). I know this is a pretty dense update, but I enjoyed talking through our design choices and the evolution of one of our most iconic classes. I had to leave a lot out, including a wide array of cut skills and spells, but I hope you enjoyed this inside look into how we iterate on our class design! Thanks for tuning in!

The Ranks tab of the Unit Window exists to allow you to reference the specifics of a unit's class rank or weapon rank. notes.title: Weekly Update #91: Soaring into 2025
notes.notes:
Hey all! 2024 has come and gone, so I wanted to take a look back and do an informal retrospective kind of update. Crystal Horizons is now entering it's third year of development, and it hasn't all been smooth sailing, but we're still proud of how far we've come and excited to keep going!

Early in 2024, we revealed the Berserker and Occultist classes. With these two additions, the number of revealed classes rose to nine, with Templar also being introduced late in 2024 to round that number up to ten. We talked about a wide variety of game systems, showed off a ton of redesigns and improvements to our UI, and even got some of our important named systems up and running (the Deployment Phase and Glossary come to mind).

We got to show off our amazing key art in the middle of the year, and take it alongside a build of the game to AVCon for more feedback and marketing. Thanks to that experience, we were able to hone in on what was and wasn't working about our class design and make adjustments. Reception to Crystal Horizons has been almost universally positive so far, which has been a big relief to us, as we believe our gameplay and class design are the most important pillars of the game.

Not everything went according to plan, though. We've missed dates we wanted to hit on multiple occasions now, especially in regards to holding the closed beta test we've been planning. As a new team working on their first real professional project, we've made some mistakes when it comes to time estimation and development throughput. A project like this is a massive undertaking, one which would be beyond the scope of most new teams. Still, we truly believe in our vision for Crystal Horizons and know that even if development isn't as fast or easy as we would like, we have no regrets and are ready to see it through.

Late 2024 was difficult for us. Problems with the project were adding up, and the closed beta we were so excited to hold had to keep being pushed back. Systems and game mechanics we had talked about were in various stages of implementation (and still are), often in a state where we're not quite able to show them off in updates. Add on the fact that we had been working on the project for 2 years without a real break, and we had a recipe for disaster. So, we made the decision to pause the weekly updates and take a break over the holiday season, hoping to come back with clear minds and renewed vigor.

I'm confident this was the right call; we've already managed to make some big progress on things we were stuck on last year after only two days back. Development is back on at full speed, hopefully with some awesome things to share soon! We have big plans for getting the project back on track and touching up all the things we left half-done, so look forward to new updates coming soon! Thanks for your continued support of Team Whirlwind and Crystal Horizons!

notes.notes:
Hey all! This week I wanted to make sure we showed off something completely new! While it's still very early in development, and I can only show you the sprite today, I wanted to reveal a new class. It's been a long time since our last reveal, and we've purposely not revealed anything for a while since we're still working on finishing up our 8 beta classes, but something new to spice things up never hurt anyone, right?

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44901040/07261e3a44e9c8052dc04b42f4a24522f4d1ee18.png

So, without further ado, allow me to introduce to you the Templar class! You can think of them as something between a Knight and a Lumimancer, but like every class in Crystal Horizons, Templars have their own unique gameplay style. Here's some quick info on the class:

Weapons: Sword, Greatsword
Armor: Heavy
Shield: Yes
Magic: Light, Healing
Brief Description: Highly adaptable frontline class with strong physical and magical defenses and decent strength. Has a number of skills and spells that are effective against magic users, such as inflicting Silence or draining MP. Can also provide support and some healing to allies.

Sounds pretty cool, right? I'm sure it would look even cooler, but I'm very limited in what I can show off today. Another notable facet of Templar is it's unlock condition: In order to reclass to Templar, the unit will require both Lumimancer at Rank 5 and Knight at Rank 3. While both Lumimancer and Knight are required to unlock Templar, that doesn't mean that Templar is automatically the better option. All of our classes are designed to be as close to evenly balanced as possible, whether they are base classes or unlockables. Generally, we've tried to increase how specialised unlockable classes are, giving them more unique and potentially stronger options but making them more situational or difficult to maintain optimal performance on. We'll be watching very closely how these classes perform once players have their hands on them.

Speaking of which, Templar (and Occultist, who we've introduced before) will not be a playable class in the (still) upcoming closed beta. notes.title: Weekly Update #85: Elemental Reactions
notes.notes:
Hey all! It's time I talked a little bit about a system we've mentioned here and there many times, and one we are considering one of the strongest hooks of Crystal Horizons: Elemental Reactions! We've been quiet on this one for a variety of reasons, and I still can't share too much right now, but I can share some screenshots and a brief introduction to the mechanic.

So, the name sounds pretty self-explanatory, but an Elemental Reaction occurs when a specific element is applied to a tile. Usually, this is through a skill or spell, or maybe a specific item. Let's use Pyromancer's Blaze spell as an example: This spell deals Fire damage in a plus-shaped area. Not only does this deal damage to any units within the area, it also applies the Fire element to all the tiles within the area.

Now that we have our applied element, which we call the catalyst, we check to see if the tile's current state has any possible reactions from a fire catalyst. For a Grass tile, we get the Burn reaction, which sets the tile alight with flame, which I'm sure many of you are familiar with already. Along with changing the tile state, the reaction will also affect nearby units in some way, like dealing damage or applying a status effect. Today, I'll be briefly introducing two new possible reactions, and talking about further reactions that can be performed from them.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44901040/9124f1310b954b57691ac0c692260614e3fba668.png

First, applying the Earth element to a Stone tile will scatter sharp stones around the tile, changing the tile state to Rocky. Similar to Burning, this tile state will deal damage units, but rather than dealing damage at the start of their turn it will instead deal an amount of damage when walking onto the tile. This means the damage can add up pretty fast if a unit walks through a bunch of Rocky tiles all at once.

Further applying the Lightning element to a Rocky tile performs a Magnetize reaction, changing the tile state to Magnastones. These are much more potent than the rocks from Rocky, and offer some additional powerful reactions. I won't reveal what these reactions are today; we want there to be some sense of discovery as players experiment with different elements, but I will say that any reactions from Magnastones will reset the tile state. We've tried to design our reaction trees to be engaging and rewarding, but not too complex or so powerful as to become the dominant strategy.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44901040/bb5a28a89b8abd746e32d0e548a8140b96d84aba.png

The other reaction I'll touch on today is Steam. This one can be achieved in two different ways; applying Fire to a Water tile, or applying Water to a Burning tile. On reaction, units on the reacting tile and adjacent tiles will take some Fire damage, and a steam cloud will be created on the reacting tile. This Steam will block line-of-sight, required for some actions, and can be further reacted upon.

From Steam, applying the Ice element will perform a Crystallize reaction, dealing Ice damage to any unit on the tile and changing the tile state to Ice Crystals. Like Magnastones, I can't go into more detail right now, but I hope you all look forward to playing around with elemental reactions when you get your hands on Crystal Horizons! We've put a massive amount of time and effort into designing the different paths you can go down with reactions, and hope finding them all will be a super fun experience! Thanks for tuning in!

Our Display and Audio settings are relatively standard as far as things go, but I'd like to talk a little bit about things found in our Gameplay and Visibility categories. Under Gameplay, our first setting determines what happens once the turn of a unit under the player's control begins. Currently, the cursor jumps to the new unit, and remains on the map. With this setting, it can instead immediately open the first level of the Action Menu, cutting out an initial button press. We've had some feedback on this and wanted to make sure we implemented it, so here it is! We also have settings to change which direction is north for the Grid Cursor, as well as the speed the cursor moves when holding a direction or using an analog stick (the Free Cursor).

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44901040/6a845be65b2dcdd79ada44240920f00b0a1c7c0c.png

Visual aids like a grid overlay and permanent team-coloured outlines can help mitigate confusion while playing, but can also add to the visual clutter at times, so we give players the choice of how they want these to be accessed. Tactical View is a mechanic that's been in Crystal Horizons for a long time, but I just came up with a cool name for it recently. By holding the Tactical View button, you can see unit health bars, expanded information on the Tile Info Panel, and whatever else you choose to toggle on in Visibility settings!

notes.title: Weekly Update #82: Stormcaller Statuses
notes.notes:
Hey all! This week, I'll be sharing the status icons for the Stormcaller class, both in an in-game screenshot and posted individually! Stormcaller has three unique class-specific status effects: Feathered, Static and Energized. I've talked about these effects before, but here's a quick refresher.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44901040/4e253e31c06df026542717a4918f31df07ae0850.png
Feathered is a debuff applied to enemies upon being hit by certain spells. While affected by Feathered, lightning spells from Stormcallers are guaranteed to land on the unit, offsetting their otherwise lower accuracy. Some spells also have additional effects when Feathered is applied, such as Chain Lightning having being able to chain to Feathered enemies from further away.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44901040/c2d87cf9a43b446f2da13955d67af575ea0ba61b.png
Static is a stackable buff applied by Stormcaller's Static Discharge passive. Upon moving, one stack of Static is granted for each tile moved through. Static increases the damage of the next action, but falls off at the end of the turn, so be sure to move first and then attack!

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44901040/7d0936634d5076f609eef3fcf235774e26237568.png
Energized is another stackable buff granted upon consuming Static, granting one stack of Energized after the enhanced action. Energized grants a ramping speed boost, making the Stormcaller faster and faster over the course of the battle. However, if two turns pass without consuming Static for an action, all stacks of Energized are lost, so be sure to keep up the offensive!

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44901040/f08d62d44c350580f773b195507d98e37991ca7f.png

In the screenshot, you'll likely have noticed that the portrait is a bit unusual. I've included the silhouette of the currently in-progress Stormcaller portrait, as it's coming along well and should be finished soon. It's been a while since the last time a portrait or key art was shown off, and that's mainly due to how small our team is. With only four core members, we all have to wear a lot of hats, so different jobs get reprioritized all the time. Currently, we're extremely focused on programming tasks for the beta, so art, alongside other parts of the game, are currently lower priority. We're certain that the work we're putting in will be worth it, so please look forward to it!

What would a fantasy setting be without a sword? Simple and reliable, the sword has a respectable statline and a set of useful Weaponskills that allow its wielder to tackle any challenge! With the unblockable Sunder to break through defensive targets, the two-hit Follow Through to cut down lightly armoured enemies, and the ranged line attack Sword Wave, you can trust this blade to never let you down!

Greatsword
{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44901040/3774f1af1f3009c8fd2fead1d3aa98f8ddb61f42.png
Wielded by Knight, Berserker, ???
Who doesn't love a big sword? Greatswords have higher base damage than the standard sword, but have a focus on dealing very high single-target damage, lacking the flexibility that other weapons have in the Weaponskill lists. Smash is a very simple skill, providing a high damage attack for a low FP cost. Heavy Slam is a very unique skill, dealing extremely high damage but stunning both the user and target. Greatsword is a good choice if you're interested in doing some big damage!

Spear
{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44901040/bbda5da5988935dfc3a2a3205276ecba8381d812.png
Wielded by Knight, ???, ???
Spears provide solid damage while allowing their wielders to attack from an extended range using their Weaponskills. Lunge is a core skill for the weapon, costing a very small amount of FP to do a slightly stronger attack that can hit an enemy two tiles away! Spear also showcases an example of a unit's weapon augmenting their Class Skills in some way: While a Knight has a spear equipped, their Binding Strike skill has its attack range expanded to include diagonally-adjacent tiles as well! We haven't yet revealed our premier spear wielder, but you can expect to see some more spear information when we do! 

Axe
{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44901040/4caa0105a5ebd3d51dfcb21863d8fca90dc81fa9.png
Wielded by Berserker, Occultist, ???
The Axe serves as a counterpart to the Greatsword, being similarly powerful but having Weaponskills that focus on hitting multiple targets at once. Cleave is a very inexpensive attack that hits in a horizontal line in front of the unit, allowing them to hit up to three targets at once. Alternatively, Shockwave deals damage to a target adjacent to the unit, but then also deals damage in an area behind the target! Making clever use of this weapon can allow you to spread damage across a wide area!

Dagger
{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44901040/280360a7ccd399d778daea7d328603c1c8b5d8ec.png
Wielded by Thief, Enchanter, Occultist
Dagger's Weaponskills provide a number of tricky or debilitating effects to help its wielder weaken or finish off their targets. Gut inflicts a stack of Bleed on its victim, a status that deals more damage the more times it's inflicted, with a number of classes including Thief and Occultist gaining bonuses against bleeding targets. Execute has unusually high damage for a Weaponskill, with its power increasing drastically when conditions are met, such as the target having a debuff or being low on HP.

Staff
{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44901040/9eda3890019f4d7371be09a940009d738232f3f5.png
Wielded by Lumimancer, Pyromancer, Stormcaller
Staff is a unique weapon, wielded by spellcasters and not suited for basic attacks. Its Weaponskills begin with Spirit Align, a self-target skill that converts accumulated FP into MP in order to allow the unit to continue casting spells. The other Weaponskills all serve to augment spells. For example, Swiftcast reduces the turn delay of the next spell cast, while Extendcast increases its targeting range. These use your move action for the turn, so instead of moving you can use one of these skills to add some extra functionality to your standard action.

Bow
{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44901040/cd680d4a05be064838040fc5ac323fcd69c5cdeb.png
Wielded by Archer, Stormcaller
Bows are ranged weapons, featuring a basic attack range of five tiles as opposed to one. Weaponskills for this weapon have different ranges and areas of effect, trading the reliability of the basic attack for more situational, powerful attacks. Power Shot deals increased damage but has a lower attack range, while Pierce Shot damages both the target of the attack and any targets directly behind them. Bow also has access to True Shot, one of very few attacks that cannot be evaded, making it a valuable skill when faced with classes that rely on increasing their evasion like Thief.



These aren't all the weapon types in Crystal Horizons, but we haven't revealed any classes that use the other weapons, so I'll talk about them at a later date. On the battlefield, units can switch between any weapons in their inventory once per turn, opening up strategies like having a Knight swap from Sword to Spear in order to reach an enemy just out of range, for example. Weapon switching will be a mechanic you'll be able to play around with in the beta (soon), but for now, that's all! Thanks for tuning in!

notes.title: Weekly Update #73: Elemental Resistances?
notes.notes:
Hey all! This week, I wanted to talk about another game mechanic we've not touched on much yet. Elemental Resistances provide percentage-based modifiers to incoming damage when that damage is of a specific element. This can either increase or decrease the amount of damage taken depending on the attack used. Classes in Crystal Horizons have their own Elemental Resistance modifiers, which are applied to the unit additively when that class is selected.

For an example, in some of our previous updates we've shows off the Reclass window, where relevant stats for each class are displayed. For the sake of convenience, I'll take a screenshot from a previous update, showing Lumimancer's stats at Level 10. Lumimancers receive 20% less damage from Light aspected attacks, such as other Lumimancer spells or an Archer with Light Arrows, but are vulnerable to the Dark element due to their -15% value. In the screenshot, the class also has a 5% resistance to some other elements, but we have since removed that due to some class design frameworks I'll talk about shortly.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44901040/5ead1849d8e7016419d4753e19ebff2fb72821b7.png

In terms of how total Elemental Resistance is calculated, we assume that the base unit has a 0% value in all elements. The Elemental Resistance values from the class are then added directly to those values. Equipment is then calculated and applied, and then finally any relevant status effects are applied. We're still working out exactly how we want to apply equipment and status resistances, whether that's additive or multiplicative; further testing should help us decide exactly how we want to handle it, or if we want to make any other changes to the formula.

Now, to follow up on those class design frameworks I mentioned earlier. Internally, we categorize our classes into one of five categories depending on their skills, stats, weapon availability and expected playstyle. These categories will likely not be relevant for the game itself, and are expected to be used solely for our own organisational benefit. The five categories we use are as follows: Tank, Melee Martial, Ranged Martial, Full Caster and Partial Caster. I'll briefly touch on each category and talk about where each of our revealed classes fit right now.

Tanks are designed with high survivability first, and often feature skills that allow them to control the battlefield effectively. Knight is the only class we've revealed in this category, and is the reason why I've brought this topic up in an update about Elemental Resistances. In order to help with their expected playstyle, classes in this category have the highest total Elemental Resistance across all elements. We decided that the weak multi-resist would be something exclusive to Tanks (mostly), so removed it from the classes that otherwise had it.

Melee Martial classes include Thief and Berserker; classes that primarily deal physical damage with melee weapons. Ranged Martial classes are similar, but trade some raw power for attack range. Archer is the only revealed Ranged Martial class so far. The main distinctions between Full Casters and Partial Casters are whether or not the class has the Staff weapon, and how reliant they are on casting spells and consuming MP. Lumimancer, Pyromancer and Stormcaller are considered Full Casters for this reason. Stormcaller is a unique case, as the other two are Staff only, but Stormcaller can also use Bows. Despite this, the class is still designed to primarily use spells, and have class skills that alter the functionality of Bows to achieve this.

Partial Casters are the most broad role. These are classes that utilize both physical damage and magical damage, both skills and spells. Unlike Full Casters, these classes cannot use Staves, and therefore are unable to access Staff weaponskills to recover MP or augment spell properties. Instead, these classes are expected to utilize basic attacks, weaponskills, FP-spending skills and MP-spending spells in order to balance their resource consumption and generation. Some of our most complex class designs fall into this role, including Enchanter and Occultist.

I've been very brief with my explanations here, but I primarily wanted to talk about the distribution of resistances across these categories. Tanks generally have the most resistances, Full Casters and Partial Casters have strong resistances to elements that their spells cover, and Melee Martial and Ranged Martial classes have few to no base resistances, but also no weaknesses. This doesn't account for class skills or equipment, however. While this system may make some classes weaker in some scenarios, most spellcasters have access to more than one damaging element and should be able to work around bad matchups.

I'll stop there for today; progress on getting the Closed Beta ready is going well, I'll share more info next week as we come closer to the date we initially projected. With that, thanks for tuning in, and see you next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update #69: Updated Knight
notes.notes:
Hey all! For this week's update, I'd like to share some updates on our class visual design pipeline, as well as a look at a rough example of some new practices we're implementing.

The Knight is one of the first classes we ever revealed, being the only class to make an appearance in our first few weekly updates before we introduced Archer and Lumimancer. Not only was this the first class sprite shown off, but also the first class portrait I drew for Crystal Horizons. It's been a long time since, and as we're now in the process of creating our more robust V2 portraits, we've run into some slight issues.

Due to our small team and lack of experience with art, we've been mostly just winging it every time we need to create a new sprite or portrait. We try to draw the character in an action pose, and work out the details as we go. This has worked fine enough for the Chieri and Enchanter portraits, the only V2 portraits so far, but other portraits currently in progress are getting done slowly due to the poor process.

We've also had cases where not having a clear design has led to inconsistencies between the sprite and portrait, which Knight has felt more than any other class. We started with a sprite, then made the portrait which introduced new details, then remade the sprite which necessitated more changed to the portrait and so on.

This back and forth has cost us precious time and resources throughout development. So, in order to both resolve this and make development of further portraits much easier, we're now in the process of creating front and back reference art for each class. This will allow us to both have a stronger direction when creating portraits and sprites, and also allow us to share the art with you all so we can better communicate details about the design of each class or character.

Now, this probably sounds like standard practice to some of you, but Team Whirlwind counts zero professional artists among it's core team, so our art pipeline has been a major pain point all throughout development of Crystal Horizons. After everyone has worked hard to learn at least one art-related skill, we're now confident that we can implement changes like this to our development structure without significant issues. Of course, things like this might mean more delays in the short term, but we're sure that it will be highly beneficial in the long run.

With that out of the way, today I can share with you the front reference image for Knight. These are relatively simple pieces, without any of the shading or poses that go into portraits, so all members of our team can have a clear understanding of how each class is meant to look. I'll be creating these reference pieces for all current and future classes, as well as characters, so look forward to seeing more of these over the course of development!

notes.title: Weekly Update #68: Stormcaller First Look
notes.notes:
Hey all! This week, I have a very early look at the Stormcaller class! While many assets are still in development, I wanted to give you all a preview of the class, since it will be one of the eight classes playable in the closed beta! 

Stormcaller is a ranged damage dealer similar to Pyromancer, but features a very different playstyle. With access to the Staff and Bow weapons, this class can choose either to augment their spells with staff weaponskills or pick up a bow to deal consistent ranged damage while generating FP. Uniquely, their unique passive skill Conduit Arms allows them to calculate physical damage using their Magic stat, so despite being a caster they are still able to output considerable damage with bows and bow weaponskills.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44901040/4077b1aabb0f40e9a9f4b7fae9f10a870bde8e50.gif

Stormcaller can cast spells from the Aeromancy and Electromancy categories. Aeromancy features wind spells that deal less damage than lightning spells, but are able to affect the battlefield with the powerful Swirl elemental reaction, allowing other Tile Elements to be rapidly spread over a large area. Dealing wind damage with these spells also inflicts enemies with the Feathered debuff, increasing their susceptibility to lightning damage.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44901040/3d56e5a5ccabf482c89624137bcb80d80850aae3.gif

Electromancy spells are the class' primary source of damage. While they have higher potencies than wind spells, they also suffer from a much lower accuracy, making them more likely to miss. This brings us into the core gameplay loop for the class; Stormcaller's Electromancy spells are unable to miss on targets with the Feathered status. Certain spells are also augmented when attacking Feathered enemies: Chain Lightning, for example, can chain to enemies at a greater distance if they have Feathered.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44901040/fb641ac88657734f29bbb7cc93eab0532a401bf6.gif

In terms of other class mechanics, Stormcaller also features the Static Discharge and Shocking Momentum passive skills. For every tile the unit moves before attacking, they gain one stack of Static, increasing the damage of their next action this turn. When Shocking Momentum is obtained, consuming Static to deal damage converts it into Energised stacks, which provide a powerful ramping action speed boost. Through this, the class is encouraged to move around the map while engaging with the Elemental Reaction system, and maintaining Feathered on enemies in order to further increase their damage.

I'll have more details on Stormcaller's skills in coming updates; we're still working on a number of assets for the class, including portrait, class icon, status icons and visual effects. I hope you enjoyed this brief peek into a new class, and I look forward to showing you all more as we continue development on it! Thanks for tuning in, see you next week!

notes.title: Weekly Update #66: AVCon Class Performance Review
notes.notes:
Hey all! This week, I've got a bit of a look back at how each class in the AVCon build has been performing, and what we might be looking at in the future for them. Huge thanks to all who gave Crystal Horizons a shot over the weekend; we got heaps of feedback and are already in discussions for what direction the game should head from here.

To start with, Knight performed as consistently as always, taking plenty of damage and striking back with powerful basic attacks. We're overall satisfied with how the class felt to play, and how intuitive Active Defense is. We may look at some changes to the order at which they acquire skills, but don't have any major plans to change it at this stage.

Lumimancer was given a few more tools this time around, including the Blessing passive (Healing an ally grants Blessed, granting them additional healing whenever the Lumimancer deals Light damage to an enemy). This ability allowed players to perform a quick heal on an ally in danger, then continue dealing damage while passively healing the ally further, which made the class feel more fluid than before. The real star, however, was Judgement, a new single-target damage spell. Despite it's extreme MP cost, players still ended up using it a lot, draining the class of it's MP very quickly. Our intention was for Judgement to be used with the critical damage bonus from the Illuminated status, while Flash was used as a cheaper damage spell, so we may look into better communicating this or making some changes to the skill.

Enchanter made it's debut performance here, and results were all over the place. Due to it's expansive kit, we saw many ways the class could be played. Some players used it as a buff-bot, ensuring the rest of their team had haste, regen and lifesteal as often as possible. Some played it as a pure spellcaster, using Aspected Spark and Aspected Flare almost exclusively. The few times we did see a player interacting with the Cut and Tie mechanic, the class performed extremely well, so we're mostly just looking at improving communication for the class at this stage.

Thief unfortunately was lacking in this build. While the class does have the highest potential damage in the game right now, it does not feel particularly good to spend two turns just applying buffs and then doing a massive backstab. We also saw very few players interact with the Dirty Fighting skills, which are meant to be a core aspect of the class, inflicting debilitating debuffs.

I'll go on a brief tangent here to talk about Move skills. Initially, these skills, which consume the unit's movement for the turn instead of their standard action, were granted only to a focused selection of classes. Knight's Active Defense and Pyromancer's Invocation were originally designed as Move skills, as both classes are incentivized to not move for various reasons. Elemental shift skills on Archer and Enchanter were later changed from standard actions to Move actions, as the class flowed significantly better when they didn't have to spend a turn not dealing damage to switch element.

As the game has developed, we've come to appreciate Move skills as tools to massively increase the fluidity of classes, and have been implementing them on more classes to great success. Lumimancer, and other classes that wield the Staff weapon, have access to the Staff Weaponskills list which include a number of Move skills. Thief, however, we were initially very reluctant to grant a Move skill to, as the class was carefully designed and calculated to function using purely standard actions.

Recent playtests have shown us that Thief has some issues, and can be one of the less engaging classes to use. We're still early in on concepts for this, but we're looking at giving it a unique Move skill that helps blend their Dirty Fighting skills into their setup and burst backstab combo. The current damage combo involves using Fade Out to gain Elusive, increasing Critical damage, using Sharpen to empower the next basic attack, and then attacking the enemy from the rear to do tons of damage. While dealing over 100 damage in a single hit feels good, the setup turns are boring, and the class isn't interacting with the powerful debuffs applied by Rending Slash and Rupturing Strike.

Our current plan is to grant Thief access to a Move skill that can be used only after executing a Critical hit with a Dirty Fighting skill. Using this Move skill will allow the Thief to move while applying Elusive, at a shorter duration than using Fade Out. This change should allow the class to deftly weave between setting up for backstabs and applying powerful debuffs when needed. We're still working out the details, but feel pretty good about this direction for the class.

This post ended up being pretty long, so I'll stop here for today. Our next upcoming goal is the Closed Beta, invites to which will be offered to members of our Discord server! I can't give a definite time on when that will be, but we're working extremely hard to get it all ready. I'll keep you posted in future updates; until then, thanks for tuning in!

notes.title: Weekly Update #63: Weaving Blade and Magic
notes.notes:
Hey all! As promised in the last update, here's one last look at the Enchanter skillset, going into a bit more detail on each skill with some short gifs thrown in! This will be a long, relatively detailed read, so please enjoy!

To start with, classes in Crystal Horizons have a set number of roughly 15-20 skills depending on the class. 5-8 of these are available at Rank 1, with the remaining skills unlocked over time until Rank 10. Enchanter has one of the highest total skill counts in the game, at a staggering 21, with most of those being spells and very few being passive skills. Across this wide array of skills, Enchanter primarily boasts a massive number of supportive spells. Alongside support, the class offers decent damage, a small amount of healing, and a whole three elements with which it can interact with the field through Elemental Reactions.

In order to not overwhelm players with massive lists of skills, the Skills menu groups skills into categories, keeping mechanically (or thematically) similar skills within the same submenu. For Enchanter, these submenus include Aspected Magic, Conceptualization, Magic Weaving and Blade Weaving. On top of those four categories, Enchanter also gets either Sword Arts or Dagger Arts depending on their equipped primary weapon.

First, Enchanter has two passive skills: Duelist and Equilibrium. Duelist allows the Enchanter to equip a Dagger to their off-hand, granting additional base evasion for doing so. Equilibrium grants the Enchanter one of two buffs depending on the actions they take; Cut or Tie. Standard attacks grant the Cut status, while using spells grants Tie. With Cut, using a spell increases the damage of the spell by 20% and grants 15 FP after the skill resolves. With Tie, using a standard attack or Weaponskill grants an additional magic power boost and restores 15% of the unit's Max MP. Both statuses are consumed upon granting their effects, encouraging the class to weave between physical and magical skills.

Aspected Magic features offensive spells such as Aspected Spark and Aspected Flare. These spells normally do unaspected (non-elemental) damage, but while an element is Internalized (more on that soon), the element of the spell changes and some additional effects are granted. Aspected Spark is the simplest, a ranged spell that hits in a plus shape, featuring a simple damage boost with an Internalized element. Aspected Flare is more expensive, but does more damage and hits in a wider 3x3 pillar, which hits units even high above the targeted area. This additional power comes at the cost of removing the Internalized element.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44901040/71c899dce8dfa47bd98fa94d7b94e3412febbfc8.gif

The Conceptualization category features three important skills: Conceptualize Fire, Conceptualize Lightning, and Conceptualize Water. These skills are performed as Move actions, consuming the Enchanter's movement for the turn but allowing them to still take a standard action in the turn. Using a Conceptualization skill grants an Internalized element status to the unit, such as Internalized Fire. With this buff, the Enchanter's physical damage is augmented and split into 50% unaspected physical damage and 50% elemental magical damage. Conceptualization also changes the properties of skills such as Aspected Spark, Externalize and Vital Strike. Releasing a Conceptualized element can be done with Release Concept as a free action.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44901040/4411d1744bf418fe596826555ac7a87fa9e2e411.gif

Magic Weaving is where the majority of Enchanter's spells sit. Light Weave, Dark Weave and Time Weave all grant Threaded buffs to an ally within range, granting health regeneration, lifesteal, and haste (increased speed) respectively. Externalize grants a buff to an ally based on the current Internalized element. Internalized Fire would grant Realized Fire to an ally, causing them to deal additional Fire damage to any enemy they deal damage to. Mass Restitch allows the Enchanter to spread either a Threaded buff or Unraveled debuff from one unit to all other units on the same team around them. There are a number of other unique support and utility spells, which I'll not spoil just yet.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44901040/cc6d7e3584845fb54eb766b473fd426162a79337.gif

Finally, Blade Weaving holds the Enchanter's unique physical skills, such as Vital Strike and Unstitch. Vital Strike deals damage while ignoring 20% of the target's defenses, and if an element is Internalized, inflicts Elemental Resist Down for that element (such as Fire Resist Down). Unstitch also deals damage to an adjacent enemy, but inflicts Unraveled, reducing the speed of the target. Unstitch is especially potent when combined with Mass Restitch, allowing the Enchanter to spread the debuff across a large number of enemies.

That was quite a long writeup, but I hope it helps get across our concept and idea for the class! Enchanter will be one of four playable classes in the upcoming AVCon build, alongside Lumimancer, Knight and Thief. We're just over two weeks away now; I hope you're all looking forward to it as much as we are!

Some maps, such as this snow-touched one, may appear to be relatively restrictive at first glance.
